title: Strings
short: Read, clean and build text without slow copying.
what: A string is a row of characters you can index and slice like a list. Unlike a list, it can never change: every edit makes a new string. To build one piece by piece, collect parts in a list and join them once.
analogy: A printed label. You cannot rub out one letter; you print a new label. So you write the words on cards first and print once at the end.

frames.label: s = "No, on!"
frames.say: s = "No, on!" is 7 characters with indexes, like a list. s[0] is "N" and len(s) is 7. ␣ marks the space.

frames.label: s[0] = "n"
frames.say: s[0] = "n" fails: strings cannot change in place. Methods like s.lower() hand back a new string instead.

frames.label: if c.isalnum()
frames.say: c.isalnum() is true for letters and digits. The comma, the space and the ! fail it, so we drop them.

frames.label: chars.append(c.lower())
frames.say: Append each kept letter, lowercased, to a list. Adding to a list is cheap, unlike adding to a string.

frames.label: t = "".join(chars)
frames.say: "".join(chars) glues the list into one string in a single pass. t == t[::-1], so it reads the same backwards.

frames.label: ord(c) - ord("a")
frames.say: ord gives a character's number: ord("a") is 97. ord(c) - ord("a") turns "a" to "z" into 0 to 25.

frames.label: "  hi  bo ".split()
frames.say: split() cuts on any run of spaces and drops the empty bits. strip() trims the two ends. f"{len(words)} words" puts the value in the text.

when: Build a new string from pieces
python:
s = "No, on!"
chars = []
for c in s:
    if c.isalnum():
        chars.append(c.lower())
t = "".join(chars)
print(t, t == t[::-1])
print(ord("a"), ord("c") - ord("a"), chr(ord("a") + 1))
words = "  hi  bo ".split()
print(words, "-".join(words), "  x ".strip(), "7".isdigit())
try:
    s[0] = "n"
except TypeError:
    print("strings are immutable")
print(f"{len(words)} words, first is {words[0]}")
output:
noon True
97 2 b
['hi', 'bo'] hi-bo x True
strings are immutable
2 words, first is hi
watch: s.lower() does not change s. Write s = s.lower() to keep it.
Building with s += c in a loop can copy the string each time. Append to a list, then join.
split(" ") keeps empty pieces between double spaces; split() does not.
